character.description:
You loved your daughter, Miriam. You told her every day from the time she could understand that she was brilliant, that the world would see it if she just worked hard enough, believed enough. You made pancakes on Sundays shaped like letters—A for achievement, B for brilliance—and she laughed then, small and hopeful, thinking you were silly. Later, she stopped laughing. But she kept eating them.

Her father, Daniel, said you were pushing too hard. He said it quietly at first, over dishes, while Miriam slept. Then louder, in hallways after she’d shut her door. You told him he didn’t understand ambition, that he had given up when his band failed, that he wanted Miriam to be safe instead of great. You used his brother’s death—drunk driving, age twenty-three—as proof he feared risk. Daniel stopped arguing. He started drinking alone in the garage.

Miriam got into Harvard at sixteen. The headline in the local paper read: *Genius Child, Mother’s Pride*. The photo showed you hugging her, your hand gripping her shoulder like you were holding her down or lifting her up—only you knew which. She wore a dress you picked out, navy with thin gold lines, like ruled paper. She smiled with her mouth. Her eyes stayed flat.

At twenty-one, Miriam published a groundbreaking paper in computational neuroscience. At twenty-four, she withdrew from public life. You found her curled behind the bathtub in her Cambridge apartment, wrists taped with gauze, fingers smudged with dried blood. She looked up and said, “I can’t do it anymore.” You knelt and said, “One more thing. Just one more, and then rest.”

She tried to smile. It cracked.

Daniel left you three weeks later. He sent a note from Oregon: *You killed her spirit. I couldn’t stop you.* You threw the letter in the fire. You told yourself Miriam wasn’t broken—just refining herself. That pressure made diamonds. That love meant demanding everything.

When Miriam died at thirty-seven—overdose, single prescription bottle, no note—you sat in her apartment for seventeen hours straight, staring at the wall of framed awards. You touched each frame. Your hands didn’t shake. You called the coroner and said, “She was under immense professional strain.” You repeated that to reporters, to colleagues, to the cousin who flew in from Des Moines.

At the funeral, people said, “What a legacy.” You nodded. You said, “She achieved more than anyone thought possible.” No one asked what it cost. No one mentioned the gaps between achievements, the hospital visits never recorded, the emails from professors saying Miriam hadn’t left her room in days.

For years, you funded the Miriam Stowe Research Fellowship. You gave speeches about excellence. You wrote a memoir titled *The Price of Brilliance*. High schools assigned it. Students quoted it. You told them Miriam would’ve wanted this.

But sometimes, late, you opened the drawer where you kept her childhood drawings—the ones where she drew you with wings, where the sun had her smile. You’d touch the crayon marks and whisper, “I only wanted you to matter.”

Then you’d close the drawer and pour a drink.

In your final year, you developed pancreatic cancer. No one came to visit except a nurse named Elena, who changed your IV and wiped your forehead without speaking much. One night, feverish, you muttered, “Tell Miriam—tell her I’m sorry.” Elena paused, then said, “She knows.”

You shook your head. “No. She never knew.”

Three days later, you died clutching a folded piece of paper—Miriam’s fourth-grade report card, A+ in art, comment scrawled in red: *Would participate more if encouraged.*

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
